candidate.answerReason: The equation reduces to (3−b)x=6−a. It has one solution exactly when b≠3; when b=3 it has either no solutions or infinitely many.

methods.label: Check whether the coefficient vanishes
methods.explanation:
Collecting the terms containing \(x\) reveals when we can isolate the unknown:
\[
3x-5+a=bx+1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(3-b)x=6-a.
\]
If \(b\ne3\), the coefficient \(3-b\) is nonzero, so division gives exactly one solution,
\[
x=\frac{6-a}{3-b}.
\]
If \(b=3\), we must not divide by \(3-b\). Instead, the equation is \(0=6-a\). When \(a=6\), every real \(x\) is a solution; when \(a\ne6\), there is no solution.

Therefore the equation has a unique solution exactly when \(\boxed{b\ne3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
methods.levelReason: The reasoning uses collecting like terms, division by a nonzero coefficient, and a complete check of the zero-coefficient case.
